RU removes artwork after criticism over 1971, 2024 portrayal
2026-08-10T16:17:18+06:00 | RU Correspondent
https://www.thedailystar.net/news/bangladesh/news/ru-removes-artwork-after-criticism-over-1971-2024-portrayal-4244441

Rajshahi University (RU) authorities have removed an artwork from an exhibition marking the July Mass Uprising following criticism over its depiction of the 1971 Liberation War and the 2024 uprising.

Prof SM Kamruzzaman, administrator of the university’s Public Relations Office, confirmed the removal this morning.

“The picture was withdrawn in the morning. The problem arose because the artworks had not been reviewed beforehand. The administration will never tolerate anything controversial,” he said.

Criticism over the artwork began yesterday after the three-day exhibition, titled “July Mass Uprising: A Free Homeland Through Colours”, opened at the university.

RU artwork criticised over alleged portrayal of July uprising as more significant than Liberation War

The artwork depicted a clenched fist holding a weighing scale, with “71” written in red on one side and “24” in a dark colour on the other. The side marked “24” was tilted slightly downwards, which critics said suggested that the 2024 uprising was being given greater importance than the 1971 Liberation War.

The exhibition was organised by the university’s Faculty of Fine Arts to mark July Mass Uprising Day 2026. It features 80 artworks in various media produced at an art camp organised for the occasion.

Concerns over the artwork were also raised during the opening of the exhibition. Earlier, Prof Mohammad Ali, dean of the Faculty of Fine Arts, said he was unaware of the artwork as he was not on campus and had not seen the exhibits. He said the artworks had been selected through registration, with Prof Ariful Islam of the Department of Ceramics and Sculpture overseeing the process.

Prof Ariful said he had only signed a letter and that the artworks had been submitted without verification.

Prof Kamruzzaman had also said earlier that the university’s Public Relations Office was only responsible for allocating exhibition space at the Senate building and had no knowledge of the individual artworks.

The student who created the artwork, requesting anonymity, said the work was not intended to portray the July uprising as being opposed to the Liberation War.
